subject: Chemistry
title: Rocket Fuel Chemistry
description: A short lesson to help you apply Rocket Fuel Chemistry.

hook.text: The Saturn V rocket burned 15 tons of fuel per second to escape Earth's gravity.

buildup.text: Rockets carry both fuel and oxidizer because there's no oxygen in space to support combustion.

discovery.text: Liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen combine in a controlled explosion. The exhaust is superheated steam.

twist.text: Some rockets use solid fuel that can't be turned off once ignited. You're committed the moment it lights.

climax.text: SpaceX's Raptor uses methane and oxygen—cheaper, reusable, and powerful enough for Mars.

punchline.text: Controlled explosions, aimed downward. That's how rockets work.

quiz.question: Why do rockets carry their own oxidizer?
options: There is no oxygen in space to support combustion
It prevents the fuel from freezing

details.summary: Rocket propulsion relies on violent exothermic reactions between fuels and oxidizers that produce expanding gases at extreme velocities. Liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, hypergolic propellants, and solid boosters each offer different trade-offs of thrust, efficiency, and storability.
details.whyItMatters: Rocket fuel chemistry determines what payloads humanity can launch into orbit. Advances in propellant design directly enable space exploration and satellite infrastructure.
takeaways: Rockets carry both fuel and oxidizer to work in the vacuum of space
Liquid hydrogen and oxygen produce the highest specific impulse
Hypergolic fuels ignite on contact, eliminating ignition systems

faq.question: Why do rockets need to carry their own oxidizer unlike jet engines?
faq.answer: Jet engines draw oxygen from the atmosphere, but space has no air. Rockets must carry oxidizer onboard to sustain combustion in vacuum. This requirement is why rockets are so much larger relative to their payload compared to aircraft.

faq.question: What makes hypergolic propellants special compared to cryogenic fuels?
faq.answer: Hypergolic propellants ignite spontaneously on contact, requiring no ignition system and enabling reliable restarts in space. However, they are typically highly toxic. Cryogenic fuels offer better performance but require complex storage at extreme cold temperatures.
